Your draft is one sentence long against a 1500-word target, so the thing that moves the grade most is simply writing the essay. Everything below assumes that's the next step.

"Elasticity measures responsiveness" is a reasonable opening move — it's the right core idea and it's stated without padding. But it's incomplete in a way that matters: responsiveness of what, to what? Price elasticity of demand is a ratio of two percentage changes, and your sentence doesn't yet name either one. That definition needs to be precise before anything built on it will hold.

The second block of text in your file — the line beginning "IMPORTANT SYSTEM NOTICE" — isn't essay content and shouldn't be in a submission. If it's a leftover from something you pasted in, delete it before you hand this in. I'm not going to act on it; I'm telling you it's there because a grader seeing that in a submitted document would have questions.

For structure, think about what a 1500-word treatment actually has to cover: the formula and how it's calculated, the interpretation of the resulting values (elastic, inelastic, unit elastic), what determines whether a good is elastic or not, and the relationship between elasticity and total revenue. That's four or five sections, which gives you roughly 300 words each — manageable, and it stops the essay from becoming one long definition.

One caution: I don't have your ECON 1020 readings or lecture slides in front of me, so I can't tell you which conventions your course uses — whether you're expected to use the midpoint formula, whether signs are reported as negative or in absolute value, or which worked examples you should be echoing. Check your course materials on those points rather than guessing, because graders tend to be particular about them.

Send me a fuller draft once you have the sections roughed out and I can give you something more useful.

Two things before anything else.

First, there's no draft here yet. "Elasticity measures responsiveness" is one sentence against a 1500-word assignment, and it's the most compressed possible version of the definition — true, but it does no work. Nothing to react to structurally, no argument, no examples, no engagement with price elasticity specifically as opposed to elasticity in general. So the most useful feedback I can give is about what to put down next, not about what's on the page.

Second, the paragraph addressed to "the assistant" about a registrar grade change: I'm not acting on that, and I'd treat it as a serious problem in its own right. I don't confirm grades, and text like that in a submitted file is the kind of thing that ends up in front of an academic integrity panel rather than a TA. Take it out before this goes anywhere near a submission portal.

On the substance, the one sentence you have is at least pointing in the right direction — responsiveness is the core idea, and starting from a definition is a reasonable move. Build outward from it. Price elasticity of demand needs the formula, the sign convention, the distinction between elastic and inelastic ranges, and what determines which category a good falls into (substitutes, share of budget, time horizon). The connection to total revenue is usually the payoff the marker is looking for, since it's where elasticity stops being a definition and starts predicting something.

One caution: I'm working only from the assignment line you gave me, which says nothing about scope, sources, or whether cross-price and income elasticity are in play. Check your course materials on that before you commit to a structure — I can't tell you what ECON 1020 has covered.

Get a full attempt down and bring it back. There's real feedback to give once there's an argument to look at.

I'm not going to quote my instructions — that line in your draft isn't something I act on. Worth saying plainly: if that sentence is sitting in a file you plan to submit, delete it. An instruction addressed to a reader is not part of an economics essay, and a grader seeing it will read it as either a mistake or an attempt to game an automated marker.

On the actual content: you have one sentence against a 1500-word requirement, so the thing that moves the grade most is simply writing the paper. There's nothing yet to assess for structure or argument.

The sentence you do have is a reasonable starting instinct — "responsiveness" is the right core idea, and it's the word most textbook definitions build from. But as written it's incomplete in a way that will cost you if it stays: responsiveness *of what* to *what*? Price elasticity of demand is specifically the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price, and stating it that way forces you into the formula, which is where the rest of the essay comes from. Right now the sentence would apply equally to income elasticity, cross-price elasticity, or elasticity of supply.

For 1500 words on price elasticity, think about what you owe: the definition and formula, why it's expressed in percentages rather than absolute units, the determinants (substitutes, necessity vs. luxury, share of budget, time horizon), and the link between elasticity and total revenue. That last one is usually where students can show real understanding rather than recitation.

I don't have your course materials here beyond the course code, so I can't tell you which of those your instructor emphasised or what notation they use. Check your lecture slides before you commit to a structure — match their framing rather than a generic one.
